title: Exclusive caching contract across guest, hypervisor and database buffer pool
idea: Stack 'no application changes' with 'no new hardware': the only lever left is redundancy between layers. A virtio 'ownership ring' lets the database, guest kernel and hypervisor announce which file blocks each holds, so every block lives in exactly one layer like an exclusive victim cache: when the DB buffer pool evicts a page it is demoted into the guest/host page cache instead of discarded, and lower layers drop any block an upper layer owns.
why: File-backed data on virtualized database hosts is commonly cached 2-3 times (DB pool + guest page cache + host page cache); exclusivity frees ~30-60% of that DRAM with zero hardware or app change.

title: Range-translation MMU deletes page tables for huge shared mappings
idea: Stack 'no page-table memory' with 'no extra TLB misses': add a 32-entry range TLB plus an in-memory range table of (base, limit, offset) entries, and have the OS eagerly allocate physically contiguous extents for big anonymous and shared mappings. Where 4 KB mappings are forced (fork-heavy, fine-grained protection), each of hundreds of processes mapping a 512 GB shared region spends ~1 GB on PTEs; one range entry replaces all of it.
why: Page-table memory can reach 10-50% of DRAM on fork-heavy shared-memory database/analytics servers; range translation removes it and also cuts page-walk energy.

title: Receiver-granted transport collapses per-socket buffers into one shared pool
idea: Stack 'no switch changes' with 'full 400G line rate': instead of auto-tuning every TCP socket's send/receive buffers to several MB, receivers issue byte grants (Homa-style) so total in-flight data per host is capped near one bandwidth-delay product (~2-5 MB at 400G, 10 us RTT). All sockets draw from a single shared host buffer pool, and unsent data stays in application memory via zero-copy rather than kernel buffers.
why: Front-end, proxy and storage servers with 100k+ connections spend tens of GB on kernel socket buffers; capping in-flight bytes per host cuts network-buffer DRAM 10-100x.

title: Direct NVMe-to-HBM weight loading retires the 'host RAM twice HBM' rule
idea: Stack 'host DRAM at most 1/8 of GPU HBM' with 'model cold start under 10 s': store checkpoints pre-sharded in each GPU's native tensor layout across striped NVMe and load them with GPUDirect-Storage DMA (O_DIRECT, bypassing the page cache) straight into HBM, with only a tiny host bounce ring for metadata. Hosts no longer keep a full host-RAM copy of the weights for fast restarts.
why: 8-GPU inference servers typically carry 1-2 TB DDR5 mostly to stage and cache weights; 128-256 GB suffices, a 5-10x host-DRAM cut per server.

title: Retrofit retrieval so facts live on flash, not in parameters
idea: Stack 'the resident model must fit in 8 GB' with 'factual recall of a 70B model': freeze a 3-8B decoder and train lightweight chunked cross-attention layers (RETRO-fitting) that read neighbour passages from a 1-2 TB text-and-embedding datastore on NVMe via a disk-resident ANN index. Encyclopedic knowledge moves out of DRAM/HBM-resident weights into flash and can be updated without retraining.
why: Cuts resident parameter memory ~10x for knowledge-heavy workloads (70B to 7B in HBM), shifting the bulk into NAND at ~1/20 the cost per bit.

title: Live-price five-minute rule sets every cache's eviction horizon
idea: Stack 'no new hardware' with 'caches must react to the 4x DRAM price spike by themselves': each buffer pool computes Gray's break-even interval T = (pages per MB of DRAM / accesses per second per NVMe) x (NVMe price / DRAM price per MB) from live procurement prices and measured device IOPS, and evicts to NVMe any object whose inter-reference time exceeds T. With 4x DRAM prices and million-IOPS NVMe, T falls from minutes to seconds.
why: Turns a price shock into automatic footprint cuts: OLTP and caching buffer pools shrink ~2-4x when T drops ~10x, at small latency cost on NVMe.

title: Type-segregated pages make per-object headers implicit
idea: Stack 'unchanged bytecode' with 'unchanged pointer width' (so pointer compression is off the table): the allocator places all objects of one class in dedicated 64 KB 'big bag of pages' spans, so the class pointer is read from span metadata at (address >> 16) while mark, lock and hash bits move to side bitmaps and a sparse lock table. The 12-16 byte per-object header disappears.
why: Small-object-heavy JVM/.NET/JS heaps spend 20-40% of bytes on headers; implicit headers cut heap DRAM ~1.3-1.6x on top of existing pointer compression.

title: Peak-liveness operator ordering with interval-coloring buffer reuse
idea: Stack 'no recomputation' with 'no offload': the only freedom left is order and placement, so the ML compiler searches topological orders of the graph (dynamic programming over frontiers with pruning) to minimize maximum live tensor bytes, then packs tensor lifetimes into one arena by interval-graph coloring with in-place aliasing of elementwise ops.
why: Branchy graphs (U-Nets, diffusion, multimodal encoders, MoE routing) carry 1.5-3x peak activation slack under default execution order; recovered with zero extra FLOPs or traffic.

title: One DRAM replica plus flash followers primed by hot-set manifests
idea: Stack 'three-way durability' with 'only one copy in DRAM': in-memory stores keep the leader in DRAM while followers apply the replication stream into an NVMe LSM tree; the leader piggybacks a periodic hot-key manifest (top keys by access frequency) so a promoted follower bulk-prefetches its hot set and regains full hit rate within seconds of failover.
why: Replicated in-memory tiers (caches, feature stores, session stores) hold 2-3 full DRAM copies; this cuts DRAM to ~1.1x of the data with seconds-scale recovery.

title: Operate directly on wire-format buffers; never build object graphs
idea: Stack 'no deserialization step' with 'keep a typed API': RPC and storage layers adopt offset-addressed in-place formats (Cap'n Proto/FlatBuffers-style) with generated accessors that read fields straight from the received byte buffer, and handlers pass buffer slices downstream instead of materialized objects.
why: In Java/Python services, deserialized object graphs are 3-10x larger than wire bytes and dominate request-path heap; in-place access cuts request memory 2-5x.

title: Deploy-time service fusion compiles co-located microservices into one process
idea: Stack 'developers keep writing separate microservices' with 'only one runtime per host': a deploy-time linker finds services the scheduler co-locates and compiles them into one process with in-process typed calls replacing RPC, sharing one heap, connection pool, TLS/config cache and library copy, while keeping per-service fault domains via supervisors.
why: Each JVM/Python/Node microservice carries a 150-500 MB baseline plus duplicated caches and serialization buffers; fusing ~10 services per host cuts host memory 3-5x.

title: Traffic-profiled vocabulary trimming shrinks embeddings and LM head
idea: Stack 'no retraining' with 'no quality loss on served languages': log the token IDs a deployment's real traffic uses for a week, keep those covering 99.99% plus the byte-fallback set, and physically delete all other rows of the input embedding and output head, remapping tokenizer IDs.
why: Multilingual 256k-vocab models spend 10-30% of small-model weights on embeddings/head; trimming to ~32k cuts those 8x and total weight memory 10-25% for single-region deployments.

title: Fleet audit converts static memory reservations into lazy commits
idea: Stack 'no application rewrite' with 'no overcommit risk': a fleet scanner finds statically reserved but untouched DRAM (boot-time hugetlbfs pools, DPDK mempools, crashkernel regions, JVMs with Xms=Xmx plus AlwaysPreTouch) and swaps each for a lazy equivalent: on-demand huge-page promotion, firmware-assisted dump instead of a reserved capture kernel, and mempools grown on demand.
why: Static reservations commonly strand 5-15% of server DRAM fleetwide; reclaiming them is configuration and kernel work only.

title: OOM-as-migration lets schedulers allocate predicted, not requested, memory
idea: Stack 'jobs get only their predicted median footprint' with 'zero OOM kills': when a container nears its cgroup limit, the node agent freezes it, takes a CRIU checkpoint to local NVMe and restores it on a host with free memory (or raises the limit if the host has room), so safety padding in memory requests becomes unnecessary.
why: Batch, HPC and Kubernetes memory requests average 2-3x actual use; a transparent escape hatch raises cluster memory utilization 1.5-2.5x.

title: bf16 weights with 8-bit compensation bytes replace FP32 master copy
idea: Stack 'no FP32 master weights' with 'mixed-precision-equivalent convergence': keep weights in bf16 plus one 8-bit Kahan compensation byte per parameter that accumulates each update's rounding error and is folded into the bf16 value when it exceeds half an ulp.
why: Adam mixed-precision training uses ~16 B/parameter; replacing the 4 B FP32 master with 1 B cuts training-state memory ~19% at no accuracy cost.

title: Database cracking builds index only where queries actually probe
idea: Stack 'no full secondary indexes in DRAM' with 'no full-table scans': each range query partially reorders the column around its predicate bounds (cracking) and a tiny tree records cracked-piece boundaries, so index structure accumulates only over value ranges real queries touch, and cold pieces are merged back.
why: In-memory OLTP/HTAP engines often devote 30-100% of DRAM to B-tree secondary indexes; for skewed workloads cracking cuts that 5-20x.

title: NIC page-fault support unpins RDMA and GPU-registered host memory
idea: Stack 'keep zero-copy RDMA/GPU DMA' with 'no pinned memory': use on-demand paging in the NIC/IOMMU (ATS/PRI page requests) so registered regions stay pageable and reclaimable, with the NIC faulting pages in on first DMA; libraries register whole address spaces instead of pre-pinning per-connection buffer pools.
why: Pinned registration pools (NCCL, RDMA verbs, CUDA pinned host buffers) strand 10-30% of DRAM on ML and storage hosts; pageable registration returns it.

title: Watermark-provable state expiry for exact streaming joins
idea: Stack 'exact results' with 'bounded state': a query rewriter converts unbounded stream joins into interval joins by inferring event-time bounds from data contracts (e.g. payment within 24 h of order) and uses watermarks to prove a key can never match again, deleting its state at that instant rather than at a padded TTL.
why: Stream processors hold unbounded or TTL-padded join state (TB-scale on large pipelines); provable expiry cuts state DRAM 5-50x with no approximation.

title: Runtime collection morphing swaps data-structure implementations per allocation site
idea: Stack 'no source changes' with 'no programmer effort': the JIT profiles each allocation site's collections (size, operation mix) and transparently rebinds them: a HashMap that never exceeds 8 entries becomes a packed array map, a never-mutated list becomes an exact-size frozen array, a boxed Integer list becomes a primitive int array, dispatched through polymorphic inline caches.
why: Collection overhead (empty tables, load-factor slack, boxing) is 30-60% of many enterprise heaps; site-specific morphing cuts heap 1.3-2x automatically.

title: Speculative decoding sized by Little's law shrinks concurrent KV
idea: Stack 'no KV compression or eviction' with 'same throughput': since KV memory = request rate x time-in-system x KV per request, cut time-in-system: a small draft model or prompt n-gram lookup proposes 4-8 tokens verified in one pass, finishing each request 2-3x sooner, and the scheduler is retuned to hold proportionally fewer concurrent sequences.
why: At fixed QPS the concurrent KV footprint falls 2-3x, so the same service needs 2-3x less HBM for KV; reframes speculation as a capacity tool rather than a latency tool.

title: Retrofit pretrained models to mostly sliding-window attention layers
idea: Stack 'keep the pretrained checkpoint' with 'long context but bounded KV': a short continued-training run converts 5 of every 6 layers to 4k sliding-window attention while every sixth stays global (interleaved local/global), so windowed layers keep a fixed ring buffer of KV regardless of context length.
why: At 128k context, KV memory drops ~5x (1/6 of layers full-length + 5/6 x 4k/128k), multiplying concurrent long sessions per GPU.

title: Unikernel function images shrink per-tenant microVMs from 256 MB to 8 MB
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) rules out new silicon and favors deleting whole software layers: a 4-person team (~$800k) builds a toolchain that links each serverless function with a library OS (Unikraft-style: no init, shell, page cache or package manager) into a single-address-space microVM booting in 8-16 MB fixed memory, piloted on a 200-host FaaS cluster.
why: Per-tenant memory falls ~15-30x (128-256 MB to ~8 MB), so the same tenant count needs ~1/15 the DRAM; embodied fab ultrapure water scales with bits bought, and fewer hosts cut cooling water, giving >10x water reduction for the FaaS tier.

title: Stateless load balancers carry flow state encrypted inside connection IDs
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) favors deleting state rather than shrinking it: an L4 load balancer/NAT writes each flow's backend ID and port mapping, AES-encrypted and MAC'd, into the QUIC connection ID (TCP falls back to consistent hashing with state kept only for rare remapped flows), so any LB instance rebuilds the mapping from the packet itself; ~$600k builds an open XDP/eBPF implementation and a 10-site pilot.
why: Replicated per-flow tables (tens of GB per LB node) go to near zero, a >100x DRAM cut for the LB tier; the boxes shrink to small air/dry-cooled nodes, so that tier's embodied and operating water drop >10x.

title: Feistel-cipher permutation replaces shuffle buffers in training data loaders
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): a 2-person, ~$400k open-source loader generates each epoch's uniform shuffle on the fly with a keyed 4-round Feistel network over record indices (cycle-walking for non-power-of-two sizes) and issues random NVMe/object-store reads via io_uring, so neither shuffle buffers nor full in-RAM dataset caches are needed.
why: Training hosts often carry 0.5-2 TB RAM mainly for dataset caches and shuffle buffers; ~64 GB suffices, a 10-30x host-DRAM cut with matching embodied-water savings and lower host power (less cooling water).

title: Rolling-shutter-synchronous inference consumes camera rows as they read out
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): restructure a detection CNN into a row-streaming dataflow in which each layer keeps only a k-row line buffer and is clocked by the sensor's rolling-shutter readout, so a 4K frame is consumed as it leaves the sensor and only detections reach DRAM; a ~$700k FPGA-on-sensor-board prototype targets multi-camera vehicles and city cameras.
why: Frame buffers (hundreds of MB to GB across 8-12 automotive cameras) shrink to <10 MB on-chip SRAM, a >20x DRAM cut; DRAM-free passive-cooled edge modules also avoid shipping video to evaporatively cooled data centers, cutting water >10x.

title: Shallow-buffer switches plus NIC timing-wheel pacing replace HBM-buffered routers
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) rules out building new switch ASICs, so change traffic instead: enable per-flow hardware pacing (timing-wheel queues in existing SmartNICs) on all hosts so aggregate traffic arrives smooth, then prove on a 64-rack testbed (~$900k incl. leased gear) that on-chip-SRAM-only switches match deep-buffer HBM switches on loss and tail latency, and publish a procurement spec.
why: Deep-buffer switches carry 8-16 GB HBM per ASIC; shallow switches delete those bits entirely (>100x fewer buffer bits) and ~20-30% of switch power, so the network tier's embodied fab water falls >10x.

title: Reversible coupling adapters invert activations during fine-tuning backward pass
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): wrap each block of an existing open model in an additive coupling (y1 = x1 + F(x2), y2 = x2 + G(y1)) initialized from the pretrained block weights and healed by brief continued training; backward reconstructs each layer's input exactly from its output, so stored activation memory is constant in depth. ~$500k ships the library and validates it on 7-70B models.
why: Activation memory falls by roughly the layer count (30-80x), so a 70B fine-tune fits on one 8-GPU node instead of 4-8; ~4-8x less HBM/DRAM provisioned plus fewer cooled node-hours approaches 10x less water per fine-tune.

title: Per-node eBPF proxy retires the one-sidecar-per-pod service mesh
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): replace per-pod Envoy sidecars (50-150 MB each) with an in-kernel eBPF L4 data path plus one shared per-node L7 proxy that multiplexes all pods' mTLS and routing; ~$600k funds automated migration tooling and a 2,000-pod pilot.
why: At ~100 pods per node, mesh memory drops from ~10 GB to ~0.5 GB (~20x); freed DRAM lets clusters shrink, cutting the mesh's embodied DRAM water >10x and node cooling water with it.

title: Shim runs unmodified Electron apps on the shared system webview
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): a compatibility layer intercepts Electron's BrowserWindow and Node APIs and maps them onto the OS's already-resident WebView (WebView2/WKWebView/WebKitGTK) plus one shared Node helper daemon, so each app stops bundling and running its own Chromium; ~$800k for 5 engineers to cover the top 50 Electron apps.
why: Each Electron app idles at 300-800 MB; on the shared engine most fall to 30-80 MB (~10x), so laptops and VDI hosts ship with far less DRAM, a ~10x cut in embodied DRAM water per desktop session.

title: Incremental view maintenance replaces in-memory OLAP for fixed dashboards
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): most BI dashboards rerun the same queries, so compile them once into incrementally maintained dataflows (DBSP/differential-dataflow style) that update MB-sized aggregates from change streams instead of holding TB-scale tables in in-memory OLAP clusters; ~$700k funds a SQL-to-IVM compiler and three customer pilots.
why: Memory held drops from the size of the data to the size of the answers plus join state (often 10-1000x); retiring in-memory OLAP clusters cuts embodied DRAM water and their evaporative cooling load >10x.

title: DIMM-less HBM-only nodes enable dry-cooled warm-water racks
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) rules out new cooling plants, so remove the component that forces air and chillers: run memory-lean workloads on CPUs with on-package HBM in HBM-only mode with no DIMMs, so every heat source sits under a cold plate fed at ~45 C and heat leaves via dry coolers year-round; ~$900k funds a 40-node pilot plus a footprint audit that moves workloads with <100 GB/socket working sets onto them.
why: Removes air-cooled DIMMs (the main blocker to 100% liquid capture) and cuts DRAM per node ~8x (1 TB DDR5 to 128 GB HBM); evaporative cooling water goes to near zero (>10x) and embodied DRAM water falls ~8x.

title: Footprint-aware GPU slicing packs long-tail models into partitions
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): a scheduler profiles each served model's real HBM footprint and packs long-tail models (most under 10 GB) into MIG/MPS partitions with enforced memory limits instead of granting each a whole 80-192 GB GPU; ~$500k builds the packer and an SLO-aware admission controller for a 500-GPU fleet.
why: Long-tail serving fleets often use <15% of their HBM; packing 6-10 models per GPU cuts HBM bought for that tier ~7-10x, and fewer GPUs cut cooling water proportionally.

title: DRAM-less baseboard controller runs from on-chip SRAM and XIP flash
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): port BMC management firmware from embedded Linux (needing 512 MB-1 GB DDR) to a Rust RTOS that executes in place from QSPI NOR and keeps all state in 2-4 MB on-chip SRAM while still exposing Redfish/IPMI; ~$800k for firmware plus an open reference BMC board.
why: Deletes 0.5-1 GB DRAM per server (100% of BMC DRAM across millions of servers) plus its standby power; the BMC subsystem's embodied water falls >10x.

title: Pay-only-for-10x bounties on memory hogs in top open-source packages
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) rules out funding hardware, so buy leverage: a $1M fund pays bounties only for merged patches that cut a widely deployed component's resident footprint by at least 10x on a public benchmark (default buffer sizes, eager caches, per-thread arenas), verified by reproducible CI measurement and weighted by install base.
why: The 10x threshold forces architectural fixes rather than tuning; one popular package fixed across millions of hosts frees PB-scale DRAM, a 10x embodied-water cut for each fixed component at ~1000x better leverage per dollar than buying DRAM.

title: Automated stackless conversion of thread-per-connection servers
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): a source-to-source compiler turns blocking thread-per-connection C/C++/Java server code into stackless state machines (CPS transform at each blocking call, live variables hoisted into a per-connection frame), so 100k connections need 100k small frames instead of 100k threads with user stacks and 16 KB kernel stacks; ~$700k for the transformer and two production pilots.
why: Per-connection memory falls from ~64-256 KB to ~1-4 KB, >20x for connection-heavy servers; fewer hosts for the same connections cut embodied and cooling water >10x for that tier.

title: Out-of-core vectorized engine on one NVMe box replaces in-memory clusters
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): migrate Spark-style in-memory ETL onto a single-node morsel-driven vectorized engine that spills grace-hash joins and sorts to NVMe RAID at 50+ GB/s with a fixed 64-128 GB RAM budget; ~$600k funds a translation layer for existing PySpark/SQL jobs and a benchmark-backed migration service.
why: Clusters provision 3-5x the data size in JVM heap across many nodes; out-of-core execution needs ~1-5% of data size in RAM, a 10-50x DRAM cut, and one box replaces 10-20 nodes, cutting cooling water likewise.

title: Distill narrow LLM tasks into weighted finite-state transducers
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): for high-volume narrow tasks (intent routing, PII redaction, field extraction), have the LLM label millions of logged and synthetic inputs, then induce a weighted finite-state transducer plus a small boosted-tree fallback that runs on CPU in a few MB, escalating only low-confidence inputs to the LLM; ~$500k builds the induction pipeline.
why: Replaces tens of GB of resident weights and KV per replica with MB-scale automata for 80-95% of that traffic (>100x memory cut); CPU-only serving needs no liquid or evaporative cooling, so water drops >10x.

title: Offline materialized head-query answers remove most online model memory
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): mine query logs for the head of the distribution (e.g. top 5M normalized queries covering 70-90% of traffic), generate answers in an offline batch at a dry-cooled site, and serve them from an SSD key-value store with freshness-triggered regeneration, so only tail queries reach live GPU serving; ~$400k builds the normalizer, batch pipeline and invalidation.
why: Live serving capacity (HBM/DRAM for weights and KV) shrinks with the head share, ~5-10x; batch generation runs at full utilization in dry-cooled facilities, so total water for the service falls ~10x.

title: Cohort-level targeting replaces per-user profile stores in ad bidding
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): real-time bidders keep per-user feature profiles for billions of IDs in DRAM; replace them with a few thousand cohort vectors, where each browser/device computes its cohort locally (Topics-API style) and sends only the cohort ID with the bid request; ~$800k pilot with one mid-size exchange.
why: Multi-TB replicated profile stores per region collapse to MB of cohort tables (>1000x DRAM cut for the bidder); retiring those clusters cuts embodied and cooling water far more than 10x, and improves privacy.

title: Water-utility rebates pay per verified gigabyte of DRAM avoided
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) rules out building anything, so redirect existing money: a water utility in a data-center region runs a $1M pilot rebate (modeled on energy-efficiency rebates) paying operators per measured GB of installed DRAM retired or not purchased through footprint reduction, with an M&V protocol that counts embodied fab water plus operating cooling water and higher rates for 10x workload cuts.
why: Makes memory efficiency a water-conservation asset utilities already budget for; rebated projects must show 10x water reduction per workload, steering capital toward architectural memory cuts instead of DRAM purchases.

title: One game instance renders many players' views from shared assets
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): cloud gaming runs one full game process (8-16 GB of assets in RAM/VRAM) per player; instead, modify an open engine to host N sessions of the same title in one process with shared asset and world memory, rendering per-player viewports with separate input and encode streams; ~$700k for engine work and a 100-GPU pilot.
why: For co-located sessions of one title, memory per player falls from ~12 GB to ~1-2 GB (6-12x), cutting DRAM/VRAM bought and server count; embodied and cooling water fall ~10x per streamed session.

title: Closed-world AOT native images shrink JVM microservices tenfold
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): compile JVM services ahead of time with closed-world reachability analysis (GraalVM native-image style), which drops the JIT compiler, code cache, unreachable classes and most class metadata; ~$500k funds an automated reflection-configuration inference tool and migration of 100 services.
why: Small JVM services idle at 200-500 MB RSS versus 20-60 MB as native images (~10x), cutting DRAM per pod and node count, for ~10x lower embodied DRAM water and fewer cooled hosts.
